items.stem: What is petroleum?
items.answer: A mixture of hydrocarbons
items.markingKey: Crude oil is a mixture of many hydrocarbons, mainly alkanes.

items.stem: Explain how petroleum is separated into fractions in a fractionating column.
items.answer: Petroleum is vaporised; vapours rise up the column, which is hotter at the bottom; each fraction condenses at the level where the temperature is below its boiling point and is collected.
items.markingKey: 1 mark heated/vaporised; 1 mark temperature gradient; 1 mark condense at different heights by boiling point [3]

items.stem: Explain why refinery gas leaves at the top of the column.
items.answer: Its molecules are the smallest, with the lowest boiling points, so they stay as gases even at the cool top.

items.stem: Put these fractions in order of decreasing volatility: naphtha, bitumen, gasoline / petrol, refinery gas. Explain your order.
items.answer: refinery gas > gasoline / petrol > naphtha > bitumen; volatility decreases with chain length (fractions from lower in the column have longer molecules and stronger intermolecular forces).
items.markingKey: 1 mark order; 1 mark linked to chain length / intermolecular forces [2]

items.stem: Put these fractions in order of decreasing viscosity: naphtha, kerosene / paraffin, gasoline / petrol, refinery gas. Explain your order.
items.answer: kerosene / paraffin > naphtha > gasoline / petrol > refinery gas; viscosity increases with chain length (fractions from lower in the column have longer molecules and stronger intermolecular forces).
items.markingKey: 1 mark order; 1 mark linked to chain length / intermolecular forces [2]

items.stem: Ines draws a labelled diagram of a fractionating column showing where three fractions, refinery gas, kerosene / paraffin, diesel oil / gas oil, are collected. (a) Give a use of kerosene / paraffin. (b) State how volatility changes down the column. (c) Name the main constituent of natural gas and write the equation for its complete combustion.
items.answer: (a) jet fuel (b) It decreases. (c) Methane; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

items.stem: What is the main constituent of natural gas?
items.answer: methane

items.stem: Explain why bitumen is very viscous.
items.answer: Its molecules are very long, with strong intermolecular forces, so they do not flow easily.

items.stem: Explain why a fraction is described as a mixture.
items.answer: It contains hydrocarbons with a range of chain lengths and boiling points, not a single compound.

items.stem: Explain why petroleum and natural gas are described as non-renewable fuels.
items.answer: They formed over millions of years and are being used much faster than they form.

items.stem: The table shows the percentage supply from fractional distillation and the percentage demand for some fractions. refinery gas: supply 2%, demand 4%; gasoline / petrol: supply 8%, demand 30%; kerosene / paraffin: supply 12%, demand 8%; diesel oil / gas oil: supply 18%, demand 23%; fuel oil and bitumen: supply 60%, demand 35%. A refinery processes 1000 thousand tonnes of crude oil. Calculate the shortfall of petrol in thousand tonnes and explain how the refinery can meet the demand.
items.answer: 220 thousand tonnes; crack excess long-chain fractions (e.g. fuel oil) into smaller alkanes for petrol and alkenes.
items.markingKey: shortfall = (30 − 8)% × 1000 = 220 [2]; cracking of surplus heavy fractions [1]

items.stem: The table shows the percentage supply from fractional distillation and the percentage demand for some fractions. refinery gas: supply 2%, demand 4%; gasoline / petrol: supply 12%, demand 28%; kerosene / paraffin: supply 12%, demand 8%; diesel oil / gas oil: supply 20%, demand 23%; fuel oil and bitumen: supply 54%, demand 37%. A refinery processes 500 thousand tonnes of crude oil. Calculate the shortfall of petrol in thousand tonnes and explain how the refinery can meet the demand.
items.answer: 80.0 thousand tonnes; crack excess long-chain fractions (e.g. fuel oil) into smaller alkanes for petrol and alkenes.
items.markingKey: shortfall = (28 − 12)% × 500 = 80.0 [2]; cracking of surplus heavy fractions [1]

items.stem: A refinery in Madrid separates crude oil by fractional distillation. (a) Describe how fractional distillation separates petroleum. (b) State how volatility changes down the column. (c) Give one reason why burning fossil fuels causes environmental concern.
items.answer: (a) Petroleum is heated to vaporise it; the column is hot at the bottom and cooler at the top; fractions condense at different heights according to boiling point. (b) It decreases. (c) CO₂ is a greenhouse gas (climate change); SO₂ causes acid rain; CO/particulates from incomplete combustion.

items.stem: What is a polymer?
options: A small molecule with one double bond
A large molecule built up from many small units called monomers
items.answer: A large molecule built up from many small units called monomers
items.markingKey: Polymers are long-chain molecules made by joining many monomers.

items.stem: Explain why addition polymers are described as saturated even though their monomers are unsaturated.
items.answer: The C=C double bonds in the monomers open up to form C–C single bonds in the chain, so the polymer has only single bonds.

items.stem: Explain how the repeat unit of an addition polymer is related to its monomer.
items.answer: It has the same atoms as the monomer, but the C=C becomes C–C with bonds extending to neighbouring units.

items.stem: A chain of poly(phenylethene), polystyrene contains 10,000 monomer units. Calculate its relative molecular mass (Mr of phenylethene (styrene) = 104).
A chain of poly(ethene) contains 2,000 monomer units. Calculate its relative molecular mass (Mr of ethene = 28.0).

A sample of poly(phenylethene), polystyrene has an average relative molecular mass of 520,000. Calculate the average number of monomer units in each chain (Mr of phenylethene (styrene) = 104). Explain why it is described as an "average".
items.answer: 5,000; chains in a sample have different lengths.

items.stem: The monomer chloroethene is made from chemicals obtained from crude oil and is then polymerised. (a) Describe a test to show that a sample of chloroethene has been completely polymerised. (b) State the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: (a) Add aqueous bromine: stays orange (no C=C left). (b) Addition: only one product (the polymer); condensation: a small molecule such as water is also formed.

items.stem: The monomer propene is made from chemicals obtained from crude oil and is then polymerised. (a) Explain why propene can form an addition polymer. (b) Calculate the Mr of a chain containing 1000 monomer units. (c) State one property that makes the polymer suitable for its use. (d) Describe a test to show that a sample of propene has been completely polymerised.
items.answer: (a) It has a C=C double bond (unsaturated). (b) 42,000 (c) e.g. flexible/strong/waterproof/unreactive/electrical insulator. (d) Add aqueous bromine: stays orange (no C=C left).

items.stem: Which type of monomer forms addition polymers?
items.answer: an alkene (contains C=C)
items.markingKey: The C=C bond opens and monomers join.

items.stem: Explain why poly(ethene) does not decolourise aqueous bromine but ethene does.
items.answer: Poly(ethene) has no C=C bonds (saturated), so no addition can occur.

items.stem: Explain why the empirical formula of poly(ethene) is the same as that of ethene.
items.answer: Polymerisation joins monomers without losing atoms, so the ratio C:H stays 1:2 (CH₂).

items.stem: Felix says that poly(ethene) is an alkene because it is made from ethene. Explain the error.
items.answer: The polymer is saturated: no C=C bonds remain.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies error; 1 mark correct chemistry [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the empirical formula of poly(ethene) is the same as that of ethene. (b) Explain why addition polymers are described as saturated even though their monomers are unsaturated.
items.answer: (a) Polymerisation joins monomers without losing atoms, so the ratio C:H stays 1:2 (CH₂). (b) The C=C double bonds in the monomers open up to form C–C single bonds in the chain, so the polymer has only single bonds.

items.stem: Name the polymer formed from but-1-ene and give one use.
items.answer: poly(but-1-ene); hot-water pipes

items.stem: A chain of poly(ethene) contains 20,000 monomer units. Calculate its relative molecular mass (Mr of ethene = 28.0).
Write an equation for the formation of poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE from tetrafluoroethene, showing the repeat unit, and explain why this is called addition polymerisation.
items.answer: n CF₂=CF₂ → –[CF₂–CF₂]ₙ–; monomers add together through the opened C=C bonds and no other product forms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark n monomer; 1 mark repeat unit with ext. bonds; 1 mark explanation [3]

items.stem: A sample of poly(ethene) has an average relative molecular mass of 14,000. Calculate the average number of monomer units in each chain (Mr of ethene = 28.0). Explain why it is described as an "average".
items.answer: 500; chains in a sample have different lengths.

items.stem: A factory in Mexico City makes poly(ethene) from ethene, CH₂=CH₂. (a) State the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation. (b) Explain why the polymer is non-biodegradable.
items.answer: (a) Addition: only one product (the polymer); condensation: a small molecule such as water is also formed. (b) Microorganisms cannot break the strong C–C bonds of the chain; it is unreactive.

items.stem: A factory in Mumbai makes poly(chloroethene), PVC from chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl. (a) Calculate the Mr of a chain containing 1000 monomer units. (b) State one property that makes the polymer suitable for its use. (c) Describe a test to show that a sample of chloroethene has been completely polymerised.
items.answer: (a) 62,500 (b) e.g. flexible/strong/waterproof/unreactive/electrical insulator. (c) Add aqueous bromine: stays orange (no C=C left).

items.stem: Which linkage is found in nylon?
items.answer: amide linkage

items.stem: Explain why each monomer used to make nylon must have two functional groups.
items.answer: A functional group at each end lets the monomer link to two others, so the chain can keep growing.

items.stem: Compare the structures of nylon and proteins.
items.answer: Both have amide links; nylon is made from two different monomers (diamine + dicarboxylic acid) repeating, proteins from many different amino acids.

items.stem: A polyester is made from HOOC–□–COOH and HO–■–OH. Describe the repeat unit and name the linkage and the other product. Name a common polyester.
items.answer: Repeat unit –[CO–□–CO–O–■–O]–; ester linkage –COO–; water; PET.
items.markingKey: 1 mark repeat unit; 1 mark ester link; 1 mark water; 1 mark PET [4]

items.stem: A polyamide is made from HOOC–□–COOH and H₂N–■–NH₂ (□ and ■ represent carbon chains). Describe the repeat unit and name the linkage and the other product.
items.answer: Repeat unit –[CO–□–CO–NH–■–NH]–; amide linkage –CONH–; water is eliminated.
items.markingKey: 1 mark repeat unit; 1 mark amide link; 1 mark water [3]

items.stem: Protein is a natural polyamide used for enzymes, muscle and hair in living things. (a) Name the type of polymerisation used to form protein. (b) State the monomers used to make protein. (c) Describe the repeat unit using block diagrams for the carbon chains.
items.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b) amino acids (c) –[NH–CHR–CO]– (different R groups)

items.stem: Explain why PET can be recycled into new PET by converting it back to monomers.
items.answer: The ester links can be broken (hydrolysed/depolymerised) to regenerate the monomers, which are then repolymerised.

items.stem: Explain the difference between addition and condensation polymerisation.
items.answer: Addition: alkene monomers join, polymer is the only product. Condensation: monomers with two functional groups join, eliminating water (or HCl).

items.stem: Compare protein and nylon in terms of the type of monomers, the linkage formed and the small molecule eliminated.
items.answer: protein: amino acids, amide (peptide, –CONH–), water; nylon: a dicarboxylic acid and a diamine, amide (–CONH–), water.
items.markingKey: 1 mark monomers; 1 mark linkage; 1 mark small molecule [3]

items.stem: A polypeptide is made from 500 molecules of the amino acid alanine (Mr = 89). Calculate the number of water molecules eliminated and the Mr of the polypeptide.
A polypeptide is made from 50 molecules of the amino acid alanine (Mr = 89). Calculate the number of water molecules eliminated and the Mr of the polypeptide.

A textile company in Bogotá produces fibres of PET. (a) State the monomers used to make PET. (b) Name the small molecule eliminated. (c) Describe the repeat unit using block diagrams for the carbon chains.
items.answer: (a) a dicarboxylic acid and a diol (b) water (c) –[CO–□–CO–O–■–O]–

items.stem: Noah compares the structures of protein and poly(ethene). (a) Name the type of polymerisation used to form protein. (b) State the monomers used to make protein. (c) Explain one difference between the formation of protein and of poly(ethene). (d) Describe the repeat unit using block diagrams for the carbon chains.
items.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b) amino acids (c) Poly(ethene) forms by addition of alkene monomers with no other product; this polymer forms by condensation, eliminating water. (d) –[NH–CHR–CO]– (different R groups)

items.stem: Why do plastics cause disposal problems?
items.answer: Most are non-biodegradable
items.markingKey: Microorganisms cannot break them down, so they persist.

items.stem: Which toxic gas can be produced when PVC is burned?
items.answer: hydrogen chloride
items.markingKey: PVC contains chlorine; incineration releases HCl.

items.stem: Explain why burning plastics is not an ideal solution to plastic waste.
items.answer: It releases CO₂ (climate change) and can release toxic gases such as HCl or CO; though energy can be recovered.

items.stem: A country produces 2.40 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 35% is recycled, 25% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 10 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 0.960 million tonnes per year; 9.60 million tonnes in 10 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: Kenji carries out a survey of plastic waste on a beach. (a) Name the type of polymer PET is and its linkage. (b) Suggest one advantage of incineration compared with landfill.
items.answer: (a) Condensation polymer — polyester; ester linkage. (b) Energy can be recovered as electricity; reduces land use.

items.stem: How can PET be recycled into new PET?
options: It is burned to release monomers
It is converted back into monomers, which are repolymerised
items.answer: It is converted back into monomers, which are repolymerised

items.stem: A country produces 3.60 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 25% is recycled, 30% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 5 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 1.62 million tonnes per year; 8.10 million tonnes in 5 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: A country produces 2.40 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 35% is recycled, 20% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 5 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 1.08 million tonnes per year; 5.40 million tonnes in 5 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: A country produces 12.0 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 12% is recycled, 20% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 5 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 8.16 million tonnes per year; 40.8 million tonnes in 5 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: Mei carries out a survey of plastic waste on a beach. (a) Give two properties of plastics that make them suitable for packaging. (b) Explain why plastic waste persists in the environment.
items.answer: (a) Low density; strong; unreactive/does not corrode; waterproof; can be moulded. (b) Most plastics are non-biodegradable; microorganisms cannot break them down.

items.stem: How does the boiling point of the fractions change from the top to the bottom of the fractionating column?
items.answer: It increases
items.markingKey: Larger molecules with higher boiling points condense lower down where it is hotter.

items.stem: Compare the gasoline / petrol and naphtha fractions in terms of chain length, boiling point and where they are collected in the column.
items.answer: Gasoline / petrol (C5–C10) has shorter chains, a lower boiling point and is collected higher up the column than naphtha (C5–C10).

items.stem: Put these fractions in order of decreasing boiling point: fuel oil, gasoline / petrol, bitumen, kerosene / paraffin. Explain your order.
items.answer: bitumen > fuel oil > kerosene / paraffin > gasoline / petrol; boiling point increases with chain length (fractions from lower in the column have longer molecules and stronger intermolecular forces).
items.markingKey: 1 mark order; 1 mark linked to chain length / intermolecular forces [2]

items.stem: Petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels and important sources of chemicals. (a) State how volatility changes down the column. (b) Name the main constituent of natural gas and write the equation for its complete combustion.
items.answer: (a) It decreases. (b) Methane; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O

items.stem: A refinery in Manila separates crude oil by fractional distillation. (a) State the approximate number of carbon atoms in molecules of gasoline / petrol. (b) Name the main constituent of natural gas and write the equation for its complete combustion. (c) Give one reason why burning fossil fuels causes environmental concern.
items.answer: (a) C5–C10 (b) Methane; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (c) CO₂ is a greenhouse gas (climate change); SO₂ causes acid rain; CO/particulates from incomplete combustion.

items.stem: What is the only product of addition polymerisation?
items.answer: the polymer
items.markingKey: No small molecule is lost, unlike condensation polymerisation.

items.stem: Tomás draws the repeat unit of poly(ethene) with a C=C double bond. Explain the error.
items.answer: The double bond opens during polymerisation; the repeat unit has only C–C single bonds with continuation bonds at each end.

items.stem: Name the polymer formed from phenylethene (styrene) and give one use.
items.answer: poly(phenylethene), polystyrene; packaging and insulation

items.stem: Jonas compares the structures of protein and poly(ethene). (a) Name the type of polymerisation used to form protein. (b) State the monomers used to make protein. (c) Name the linkage in protein. (d) Explain why proteins are broken down in the body but nylon is not.
items.answer: (a) Condensation polymerisation. (b) amino acids (c) amide (peptide, –CONH–) (d) Enzymes hydrolyse the amide links in proteins; no enzymes break nylon down.

items.stem: Explain why plastic waste in the oceans is a problem.
items.answer: It persists for years; animals eat it or become entangled; microplastics enter food chains.

items.stem: Explain why the same properties that make plastics useful also cause disposal problems.
items.answer: Their unreactivity and strength mean they do not break down/biodegrade in the environment.

items.stem: A country produces 8.00 million tonnes of plastic waste each year: 25% is recycled, 40% is incinerated and the rest goes to landfill. Calculate the mass sent to landfill each year and the total over 10 years, and suggest one way to reduce it.
items.answer: 2.80 million tonnes per year; 28.0 million tonnes in 10 years; increase recycling / use biodegradable plastics / reduce single-use plastics.

items.stem: Explain why plastics must be sorted before recycling.
items.answer: Different polymers have different structures and properties, and must be processed separately.

items.stem: A council in Kathmandu is choosing between landfill and dumping in the ocean for its plastic waste. Give one disadvantage of each.
items.answer: Landfill: plastics are non-biodegradable and take up space for hundreds of years. Dumping in the ocean: harms marine animals that swallow or become trapped in plastic; microplastics enter food chains.
